transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-10-03
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 58 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Jordan Patel (Redwood SE); Priya Rao (Lacuna Head of Platform); Ethan Morgan (Lacuna Director of ML); Sofia Velasquez (Lacuna FinOps)

Summary:
Quick intake to understand Lacuna's hosting tradeoffs: per-token cost tolerance, expected throughput, and whether Hosted, Dedicated or Private makes sense for their roadmap. Focus on batching/caching levers, residency/SOC2 concerns, and a short plan to run a small benchmark/pilot.

Topics discussed:
- Current stack and traffic profile
- Cost targets and acceptable latency thresholds
- Batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization levers
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) decision criteria
- Next steps and benchmarks

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round-robin we got Maya and Jordan from Redwood, and I think Priya, Ethan, Sofia with Lacuna. Good to see you all.
[00:12] Priya Rao: Hey, yep, thanks for setting this up. We have about an hour, hopefully we can get through the high-level economics and then the SE bits.
[00:22] Jordan Patel: Sounds good. I'll mostly be the technical neighbor here, I can dive into latency and batching tradeoffs.
[00:30] Ethan Morgan: To set context, our product is an inline assistant that annotates docs and generates short summaries, so median prompt lengths are small — 80 to 150 tokens — but we do have spikes for longer summarizations.
[00:45] Sofia Velasquez: From FinOps, our primary constraint is budget. We're trying to keep incremental inference spend below $25k/month initially, and that includes both hosted API and any dedicated reserved capacity.
[00:58] Maya Chen: Got it. So cost target of ~25k. Are you expecting predictable steady-state throughput or large spiky peaks?
[01:05] Priya Rao: It's spiky. We have daily bursts when customers batch documents overnight and then some real-time interactive usage during the day. Spikes can be 4-5x baseline for a couple hours.
[01:20] Jordan Patel: Ok, that pattern favors a hybrid: baseline routed to Dedicated or Private reserved capacity and bursts absorbed by Hosted (or burst pools) — that keeps unit cost lower while avoiding cold starts. 
[01:34] Ethan Morgan: When you say unit cost lower, can you quantify? Like per-token difference between hosted and dedicated?
[01:40] Maya Chen: Rough ballpark: hosted API is simpler and you pay per-token + margin; dedicated reserved capacity converts spend into GPU-hour style commits which typically lower per-token cost for high-volume workloads. For example, for a 13B-class model hosted might be $0.00012 per token for generation whereas a dedicated path could drop that to $0.00006-$0.00009 depending on utilization and batching.
[02:03] Sofia Velasquez: That's a big range — what's driving the spread?
[02:07] Jordan Patel: The big levers are batching efficiency (how many concurrent requests can be combined), prefix/KV cache hit rates (if many requests share common context), quantization and model variant selection, and also the chosen sequence length distribution. If you can get high batching and cache hits, effective per-token cost halves or more.
[02:26] Priya Rao: Quick question — our prompts often start with a fixed policy header (~120 tokens) then a variable doc. Is that the kind of pattern that benefits from prefix caching?
[02:35] Jordan Patel: Absolutely. That's classic prefix caching use-case: the static header is cached in the KV cache so for repeated calls the runtime only attends to appended tokens. If you get high reuse, you save compute per request. Note: prefix caching efficacy depends on model architecture and whether you're using continuous batching and how long the cache persists.
[02:54] Ethan Morgan: You mentioned quantization — do we need to retrain or is it a serving-only setting?
[03:00] Jordan Patel: Mostly serving-only. We offer quantized model variants (int8, 4-bit variants) that run faster and cheaper; quality can be model and prompt dependent. We usually recommend running a small eval suite to verify regressions.
[03:15] Sofia Velasquez: For budget modeling, we need a simple TCO view: estimated monthly tokens * per-token cost + any Dedicated commit amortized. Can Redwood provide a template?
[03:25] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share a cost model template. We'll need your expected QPS, typical prompt + generation lengths, and your percent of cached prefixes.
[03:33] Priya Rao: We can provide 14 days of telemetry.
[03:36] Priya Rao: One more thing — we have SOC2 Type II but some customers require data residency and strict KMS control. If we go Hosted, does Redwood offer KMS integration and VPC peering?
[03:47] Maya Chen: Hosted offers encrypted-at-rest and in-transit data on our side, but for tight control you can use Dedicated or Private which let you bring your own KMS and run in VPCs or on-prem. Hosted has options for customer-managed keys in certain enterprise tiers; we can include that in the security packet.
[04:02] Ethan Morgan: Latency targets — we need p95 under 350ms for short completions (<=128 tokens). Is that achievable on hosted?
[04:10] Jordan Patel: P95 under 350ms is feasible for small completions on hosted if your traffic fits within the latency SLO and model choice. Key dependencies: batching window (we tune for low latency), warm KV caches, and the model size. Larger models increase latency.
[04:28] Maya Chen: Also note the routing policy — if you route to dedicated instances in the same region you avoid cross-region penalties. Hosted multi-region fallback can add variability.
[04:38] Sofia Velasquez: Let's talk numbers. If we assume 20M tokens/month and 70% of calls benefit from a 50% cache saving, what ballpark monthly spend are we looking at on hosted vs dedicated?
[04:52] Jordan Patel: Quick rough math — hosted at $0.00012/token * 20M = $2,400. Wait that seems off. Sorry, mis-said — that's generation-only? Let me re-calc: if average total tokens per request (prompt + gen) is 200, and 20M tokens is your token budget, hosted raw would be 20M * $0.00012 = $2,400 in model compute. With caching and batching you reduce effective tokens; if 70% see 50% reduction that's like 20M - 7M = 13M effective tokens -> $1,560. Dedicated could be lower if you commit and achieve high utilization, maybe $1,000-$1,400 after amortized GPU hours.
[05:34] Sofia Velasquez: Hmm those are smaller numbers — I thought our spend was higher, maybe I'm mixing request count with tokens.
[05:40] Priya Rao: Right, we track requests: 1.5M requests/month, average 180 tokens per request -> ~270M tokens/month. Sorry earlier number was off.
[05:52] Maya Chen: Ok that changes things. 270M tokens at $0.00012 = $32,400 hosted baseline. With a 50% effective cache on 70% of calls, that's roughly (0.7*0.5*270M saved = 94.5M saved) -> effective tokens 175.5M -> ~21k hosted. Dedicated could push it lower to maybe $12k-$16k depending on utilization and the committed GPU pricing.
[06:21] Sofia Velasquez: That aligns more with our finance model. Does dedicated require a 12-month commit?
[06:26] Maya Chen: Typical plans are monthly or annual reserved pools. We have monthly reserved capacity with a modest uplift, annual gives best rate. There's also burst policies so you can overflow to hosted at higher per-token rates during spikes.
[06:40] Ethan Morgan: For the benchmark you suggested — what's the best minimal experiment to prove economics?
[06:46] Jordan Patel: Two-pronged: 1) run a 48-hour hosted test with traffic replay from your logs to capture burst behavior, and 2) run a small dedicated cluster (2-4 GPUs) with identical work to compare latency and cost at measured utilization. We'll instrument token-level costs.
[07:01] Priya Rao: We'll need to anonymize data — can you accept a scrubbed dataset?
[07:05] Jordan Patel: Yep, scrubbed or synthetic is fine as long as token distributions and prefix patterns are maintained.
[07:12] Maya Chen: Also we'll include guidance on batching knobs — e.g., increasing batch window from 5ms to 20ms can raise throughput significantly but adds tail latency.
[07:23] Sofia Velasquez: Can you explain how batching vs caching trade when you have spikes? Like we care about p95 latency during spike windows.
[07:32] Jordan Patel: Sure — batching groups concurrent requests to improve GPU utilization. During spikes, batching becomes more effective because more concurrent requests exist, increasing batch sizes and lowering per-token compute. But it can increase p95 if you wait for batch fill. Conversely, prefix caching reduces work per request regardless of concurrency by avoiding re-computation for cached prefixes. So caching helps latency and cost at all loads, batching helps cost more at high concurrency but can hurt latency if windows increase.
[07:58] Ethan Morgan: Any tips on prompt engineering to hit better caching?
[08:02] Jordan Patel: Keep static headers as consistent as possible so they're cacheable, avoid random salts or metadata in the prompt that defeats caching. Also canonicalize timestamps and user ids outside the prompt or via separate fields.
[08:15] Priya Rao: About Private/on-prem — our security team says they prefer Private for customer X. What's the lift?
[08:22] Maya Chen: For Private deployments we provide a customer-managed control plane and options for on-prem runtime. Typical on-prem deployment takes 6-10 weeks depending on networking and cert approvals; VPC-based private deployments can be faster. Private has higher fixed costs but gives KMS control, audit logs, and residency guarantees.
[08:37] Sofia Velasquez: Okay. From cost perspective do you have a break-even calculator for Dedicated vs Private vs Hosted?
[08:44] Maya Chen: We'll include a break-even sheet. Usually Hosted is better for unpredictable, low-to-medium volume; Dedicated wins when you have sustained utilization > a given threshold (we'll compute with your telemetry); Private becomes viable when regulatory or residency needs force it, or when the scale and latency SLAs justify the fixed cost.
[09:02] Ethan Morgan: Anything we should watch out for with throttling or burst queue limits?
[09:07] Jordan Patel: We expose rate limits at token and request levels. With Reserved capacity you can configure burst pools. During very large spikes, our routing will fall back to higher-cost pool or degrade to a smaller model to preserve availability. We'll show fallback configurations in the plan.
[09:22] Priya Rao: Can you send a sample fallback policy so our SREs can review?
[09:26] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share a sample canary and fallback configuration.
[09:30] Sofia Velasquez: On the procurement side, what's the minimum contract size for Dedicated?
[09:34] Maya Chen: We can do a pilot commit for a single GPU-month equivalent or scale up. Commercial will propose options once we scope the expected committed utilization.
[09:44] Ethan Morgan: A corner case — some calls have multi-step tool calling; does Redwood charge for model token outputs only, or also for tool parsing?
[09:53] Jordan Patel: We bill per generated and input tokens processed by the model. Tool calls that trigger extra model prompts are billed accordingly. We can instrument and show token-level breakdowns per route.
[10:05] Priya Rao: Great. Anything else on the benchmark instrumentation?
[10:08] Jordan Patel: We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, avg batch size, KV cache hit rate, and per-token cost.
[10:16] Sofia Velasquez: Timeline — can we kick off benchmarks next week?
[10:19] Maya Chen: If you provide telemetry by Friday, Jordan and I can spin up the hosted replay and get a preliminary pass in 72 hours, dedicated baseline takes a few more days.
[10:28] Priya Rao: We'll extract and share by EOD Thursday. 
[10:31] Ethan Morgan: One last question — in dedicated, how quickly can we scale capacity up during growth?
[10:36] Maya Chen: We can autoscale within configured limits; reserved pools can be increased but there's provisioning lead time for large additions. For short-term bursts we recommend burst-to-hosted.
[10:46] Priya Rao: Ok let's recap next steps.
[10:48] Maya Chen: Recap: 1) Lacuna to share 14 days of scrubbed traffic and token distribution (Priya). 2) Redwood to send per-token pricing matrix and a break-even calc (Maya). 3) Redwood SE to run hosted replay + small dedicated trial and share instrumentation (Jordan). 4) Schedule a follow-up to review benchmark results (all).
[11:10] Priya Rao: That sounds good. Thanks team.
[11:15] Sofia Velasquez: Thanks.
[11:17] Maya Chen: We'll follow up with the security pack and an initial SOW for the pilot.
[11:22] Ethan Morgan: Bye all.

Post-meeting notes:
- Redwood to prioritize cost model and hosted vs dedicated runbook for Lacuna.
- Customer appears likely to pilot with a small dedicated pool + hosted overflow.
- Security/trust items (KMS, SOC2, VPC) are blocking for some enterprise customers; provide doc bundle.
